On appeal, Tekola challenged the district court’s application of a sentencing enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(b)(12). He argued that although he sold drugs from the apartment, the property’s primary purpose was as his residence. The Ninth Circuit rejected that argument and held that the district court did not abuse its discretion in applying the enhancement.
Tekola argued that the enhancement should not apply because the apartment primarily served as his residence. ## The dispute in brief
The case arose after federal investigators traced fentanyl that killed a young person in Goleta, California, to Isaac Tekola. According to the opinion, agents determined through interviews and online message records that Tekola had been selling drugs for years and frequently used his apartment as the base for those activities.
At sentencing, the district court applied a two-level enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(b)(12), concluding that Tekola had maintained the apartment for the purpose of distributing controlled substances. The court ultimately imposed a sentence of 105 months’ imprisonment.
## How the court got there
The guideline commentary clarifies that drug distribution does not have to be the sole purpose of the premises. Instead, the activity must be one of the defendant’s “primary or principal uses” of the property rather than merely an incidental use.

Tekola argued that the enhancement should not apply because the apartment primarily served as his residence. In his view, the guideline was intended to target stash houses or locations used mainly for drug distribution.

# Ninth Circuit Upholds Drug-Premises Sentencing Enhancement in United States v. Tekola

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit affirmed a federal sentencing enhancement in United States v. Tekola.
...
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit has affirmed a federal drug-trafficking sentence in United States v. Tekola, holding that a district court properly applied a sentencing enhancement for maintaining a premises used for drug distribution.

In a decision filed March 9, 2026, the court concluded that the defendant’s apartment functioned as the central hub of his drug-trafficking operation, supporting the enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(b)(12).

The ruling confirms that the enhancement may apply even when the premises used for drug trafficking also serves as the defendant’s residence.

According to the opinion, agents determined through interviews and online message records that Tekola had been selling drugs for years and frequently used his apartment as the base for those activities.

Tekola later admitted that the seized cash came from drug dealing and that a safe in his bedroom closet was used to store drugs and drug proceeds.

Messages recovered from Tekola’s phone further indicated that he conducted drug transactions from the apartment and used it as a central location for his distribution activity.

linkup.snippet:
In September 2022, fentanyl killed a young person in Goleta, California. Federal agents traced the drugs back to Isaac Tekola, who had been dealing from his apartment in the Central District of California for years.
Tekola pleaded guilty to possession with intent to distribute fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine, and Alprazolam. At sentencing, the district court imposed a two-level enhancement under U.S. Sentencing Guideline § 2D1.1(b)(12) for maintaining a premises for drug manufacturing or distribution, and sentenced Tekola to 105 months. Tekola appealed, arguing the enhancement should not apply because the apartment was his primary residence, not a “stash house.”
## The Court’s Holding  
The Ninth Circuit affirmed. The court held that the § 2D1.1(b)(12) enhancement does not require drug trafficking to be the *sole* purpose of the premises—it need only be “one of the defendant’s primary or principal uses.” Following sister circuits, the panel found that overwhelming evidence showed Tekola’s apartment was the central hub of his distribution network: he stored drugs there, processed and packaged them in his bedroom, maintained tools of the trade throughout the apartment, and regularly conducted sales from the location.  
The court distinguished its earlier decision in *United States v. Shetler*, which had interpreted the related criminal statute 21 U.S.C. § 856(a)(1) more narrowly to avoid constitutional vagueness concerns. The panel explained that those concerns do not apply to sentencing guidelines, which merely guide judicial discretion and are not subject to vagueness challenges under *Beckles v. United States* (2017). The enhancement is also narrower than the statute because it requires “maintaining” premises for “manufacturing or distributing”—not merely “using” any controlled substance.

Ninth Circuit Reinstates Suit Over Handcuffing of 11-Year-Old
By KENNETH OFGANG, Staff Writer
A Los Angeles man who was 11 years old when a team of officers allegedly pointed guns at and handcuffed him while seeking to arrest his father can sue for violation of his constitutional rights, the Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Friday.
U.S. District Judge Ronald S.W. Lew ruled two years ago that the agents, from the IRS, Drug Enforcement Administration, and Los Angeles Police Department, did not use excessive force or unreasonably detain Ephraim Tekle. The judge also ruled that to the extent there may have been a Fourth Amendment violation, the agents acted reasonably and were entitled to qualified immunity.
The Ninth Circuit panel disagreed, saying no reasonable officer would have believed that the Constitution allowed him to act in the manner Tekle alleges.
The defendants acknowledged detaining Tekle when they arrested his father on tax and drug charges at the family home. But they claimed that he looked older and that they did not know he was unarmed.
Mother Arrested
A different team of agents had earlier arrested Tekle’s mother after she dropped off his two siblings at school. Tekle testified at his deposition that he was taking out the trash, unaware of the officers’ presence, when he hear a voice over a “loud intercom” saying “turn around and put your hands in the air.”

In a decision filed March 9, 2026, the court concluded that the defendant’s apartment functioned as the central hub of his drug-trafficking operation, supporting the enhancement under U.S.S.G. § 2D1.1(b)(12).
